title: SQL Basics: Working with Data
summary: Learn to read, summarise, join and safely change data in database tables using standard SQL, and design a simple table of your own.
audience: Beginners aged 14 and up. No prior coding needed; a phone or tablet with a browser is enough

body.p: A database stores data in tables. A table looks like a page in an exercise book ruled into a grid. Each column has a name and holds one kind of fact, and each row is one record, such as one product in a shop. SQL, pronounced S-Q-L or sequel, is the language used to ask databases questions. This course uses SQLite-compatible standard SQL. Small dialect differences exist between systems such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and SQLite, so a few details may differ on the system you use, but the ideas stay the same.

You can practise on a phone or tablet using any free online SQL editor or playground in your browser. Create the tables below, run the examples and compare your results with the output shown. In this lesson we use a table called products, kept by a small shop. Prices are in naira.

body.code: SELECT * FROM products;

id | name          | category | price | stock
---+---------------+----------+-------+------
1  | Exercise book | School   | 350   | 120
2  | Pen           | School   | 100   | 300
3  | Rice 1kg      | Food     | 1500  | 40
4  | Phone credit  | Services | 500   | 999
5  | Beans 1kg     | Food     | 1200  | 25
6  | Calculator    | School   | 4500  | 8

body.p: SELECT chooses what to show and FROM says which table. The star means all columns. SQL commands are not case sensitive, but writing the keywords in capitals makes them easy to spot. Every statement ends with a semicolon. Notice that the output is one header line and then one line per row.
Most of the time you only want some columns. List their names separated by commas. You can also rename a column in the output with AS, which is called an alias.

body.code: SELECT name, price FROM products;

name          | price
--------------+------
Exercise book | 350
Pen           | 100
Rice 1kg      | 1500
Phone credit  | 500
Beans 1kg     | 1200
Calculator    | 4500
SELECT name, price * 2 AS double_price FROM products;

name          | double_price
--------------+-------------
Exercise book | 700
Pen           | 200
Rice 1kg      | 3000
Phone credit  | 1000
Beans 1kg     | 2400
Calculator    | 9000

body.p: The second query calculates a new value for each row without changing the stored data. SELECT only reads. It never alters the table.

list: INTEGER holds whole numbers such as 350.
TEXT holds words, written in single quotes such as 'Rice 1kg'.
REAL holds decimal numbers such as 12.5.
NULL means no value is known. It is not zero and not an empty text.

body.tip: Text values use single quotes. Double quotes are meant for column and table names, and some systems will reject them around text.

body.p: A table can hold thousands of rows, so you need to pick the ones you want. The WHERE clause keeps only the rows where a condition is true. It comes after FROM.

body.code:
SELECT name, price FROM products
WHERE category = 'Food';

name      | price
----------+------
Rice 1kg  | 1500
Beans 1kg | 1200

body.p: Comparison operators are =, <> (not equal), <, >, <= and >=. Notice that SQL uses a single equals sign to compare, unlike many programming languages. Combine conditions with AND, OR and NOT. AND needs both to be true, while OR needs at least one.

body.code:
SELECT name, price FROM products
WHERE category = 'School' AND price < 1000;

name          | price
--------------+------
Exercise book | 350
Pen           | 100

SELECT name, category FROM products
WHERE category = 'Food' OR price > 4000;

name       | category
-----------+---------
Rice 1kg   | Food
Beans 1kg  | Food
Calculator | School

body.p: LIKE matches text patterns. The percent sign stands for any number of characters. BETWEEN checks a range including both ends, and IN checks a list of values.

body.code: SELECT name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%1kg';

name
---------
Rice 1kg
Beans 1kg
SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price BETWEEN 300 AND 1200;

name          | price
--------------+------
Exercise book | 350
Phone credit  | 500
Beans 1kg     | 1200
SELECT name FROM products WHERE category IN ('Food', 'Services');

name
------------
Rice 1kg
Phone credit
Beans 1kg

body.p: Rows come back in no promised order unless you ask. ORDER BY sorts, from smallest to largest by default (ASC). Add DESC for largest first. LIMIT cuts the result to the first few rows, which together with ORDER BY answers questions such as: which are the two most expensive items?

body.code:
name       | price
-----------+------
Calculator | 4500
Rice 1kg   | 1500

body.p: The order of the clauses always is SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT. Writing them in another order causes an error.

body.tip: To find missing values use IS NULL, not = NULL. A comparison with NULL is never true, so = NULL finds nothing.

body.p: Sometimes you do not want rows but a summary: how many, how much, the biggest. Aggregate functions take many rows and return one value. The common ones are COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX.

body.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS items, SUM(stock) AS total_stock, MIN(price) AS cheapest, MAX(price) AS dearest
FROM products;

body.p: COUNT(*) counts rows. You can add WHERE first to summarise only some rows. The filter happens before the summary.
The average of 350, 100 and 4500 is 1650, shown here as 1650.0. How an average is displayed, for example 1650 or 1650.0, can differ between systems, which is one of the small dialect differences.
GROUP BY splits the rows into groups that share a value, then calculates the aggregate for each group. It answers questions such as: how many products are in each category?

body.code:
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS items, SUM(stock) AS units
FROM products
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY category;

category | items | units
---------+-------+------
Food     | 2     | 65
School   | 3     | 428
Services | 1     | 999

body.p: Every column in SELECT must either be in GROUP BY or be inside an aggregate function. If you select name as well, there is no single name for a group, and this is a common beginner error.
WHERE filters rows before grouping, so it cannot use an aggregate. To filter groups after they are made, use HAVING.

body.code:
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS items
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY category;

category | items
---------+------
Food     | 2
School   | 3

body.p: Food and School each have at least two products, so they stay. Services has only one, so it disappears.

body.tip: Quick memory aid: WHERE works on rows, HAVING works on groups.

body.p: Good databases split information into several tables so that nothing is repeated. A customer's name and city are stored once in a customers table. An orders table then stores only the customer's id number. The id in customers is its primary key, a value that identifies each row. The customer_id in orders is a foreign key, a column that points to a row in another table.

body.code: SELECT * FROM orders;

body.p: Reading raw ids is not friendly. Order 1 belongs to customer 1, but who is that? A JOIN combines rows from two tables where a matching condition is true. The ON part says which columns must match. Short names after the table names, called aliases, save typing.

body.code:
SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name, c.city, o.qty
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.id;

order_id | name    | city    | qty
---------+---------+---------+----
1        | Ama     | Accra   | 4
2        | Chidi   | Lagos   | 2
3        | Ama     | Accra   | 10
4        | Wanjiru | Nairobi | 1
5        | Chidi   | Lagos   | 3
6        | Mwila   | Lusaka  | 2

body.p: You can join more than two tables by repeating JOIN. Here we also fetch the product name and calculate the cost of each order. The qty column is multiplied by price.

body.code:
SELECT c.name, p.name AS product, o.qty * p.price AS cost
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id
ORDER BY cost DESC;

name    | product       | cost
--------+---------------+-----
Wanjiru | Calculator    | 4500
Chidi   | Rice 1kg      | 3000
Ama     | Exercise book | 1400
Chidi   | Exercise book | 1050
Ama     | Pen           | 1000
Mwila   | Phone credit  | 1000

body.p: A plain JOIN (also called INNER JOIN) keeps only rows that have a match on both sides. Fatmata in Freetown has not ordered anything, so she is missing from the result above. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills the missing parts with NULL.

body.code:
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

name    | order_id
--------+---------
Ama     | 1
Ama     | 3
Chidi   | 2
Chidi   | 5
Wanjiru | 4
Mwila   | 6
Fatmata | NULL

body.p: A very useful trick is to combine LEFT JOIN with WHERE ... IS NULL to find rows with no match, such as customers who never ordered.

body.code:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

name
-------
Fatmata

body.p: Joins also work with GROUP BY. For example, you can total the quantity ordered by each city, which combines everything you have learnt so far.

body.code:
SELECT c.city, SUM(o.qty) AS items_ordered
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.city
ORDER BY items_ordered DESC, c.city;

city    | items_ordered
--------+--------------
Accra   | 14
Lagos   | 5
Lusaka  | 2
Nairobi | 1

body.tip: When two tables have a column with the same name, such as id or name, put the table alias in front, like c.name, so SQL knows which one you mean.

lessons.title: Changing data safely: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE

body.p: So far you only read data. Three commands change it: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes existing rows and DELETE removes rows. These change the stored data, so treat them with care. Practise only on test data.
INSERT INTO names the table and the columns, then VALUES gives the data in the same order. Listing the columns is safer than relying on their order.
UPDATE ... SET changes the listed columns. The WHERE clause chooses which rows. Sugar has become more expensive, so we raise the price of only product 7.

body.code:
UPDATE products SET price = 1300 WHERE id = 7;

SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE id = 7;

DELETE FROM products WHERE id = 7;

SELECT COUNT(*) AS items FROM products;

items
-----
6

body.p: The count is back to the original six products.

body.h: The danger of a missing WHERE

body.p: UPDATE and DELETE without WHERE act on every row in the table. SQL will not ask whether you are sure. Imagine you meant to change one price but forgot the WHERE clause.

body.code:
UPDATE products SET price = 0;

SELECT name, price FROM products;

name          | price
--------------+------
Exercise book | 0
Pen           | 0
Rice 1kg      | 0
Phone credit  | 0
Beans 1kg     | 0
Calculator    | 0

body.p: Every product is now free, and in a real shop this would be a disaster. The same mistake with DELETE would erase the whole table's rows. Real databases protect themselves with backups and with transactions, but you should build safe habits from the start.

steps: Write the WHERE clause first, or write a SELECT with the same WHERE and check it returns exactly the rows you expect.
Only then change SELECT to UPDATE or DELETE, keeping the same WHERE.
Filter by the primary key, such as id = 7, when you mean one row.
Check the result with a SELECT afterwards.
Keep a backup or copy of data that matters.

body.tip: Typing the WHERE condition before the rest of the command is a good habit that makes forgetting it much less likely.

body.p: Before storing data, you create the table with CREATE TABLE. You name each column, give it a type, and add rules called constraints. Careful design now prevents messy data later. Imagine a school club wants a list of members.

list: PRIMARY KEY marks the column that uniquely identifies each row, so two members cannot share an id.
NOT NULL means the column must always have a value.
DEFAULT gives a value when none is supplied. Here fee_paid starts at 0.
Types such as INTEGER and TEXT are common to most systems, but names and extra types, for example VARCHAR or BOOLEAN, differ between database systems.

body.p: Let us test it. We insert two members and leave out fee_paid for one.

body.code: SELECT * FROM members;

body.p: Esi gets the default of 0, meaning not paid yet. If you tried to insert a member with no name, the database would refuse, which protects the quality of your data.

list: One table for one kind of thing: members, products, orders.
Give every table an id column as the primary key.
Do not repeat the same facts in many rows. Store a customer once and link to them using a foreign key, as the orders table does with customer_id.
Choose clear lowercase names with no spaces, such as fee_paid.
Store one fact per column. Put first name and last name in separate columns if you need to sort by either.

body.p: Here is how a foreign key is written in a table that records which member attended which meeting. It links to the members table.

Dates are stored as text in a standard form such as 2026-03-15, which sorts correctly. Date types vary between systems, another place where dialects differ. To finish, remember that you can remove a whole table with DROP TABLE, which deletes the table and all its data, so use it very carefully.

body.tip: Draw your tables on paper first: list each table, its columns, and which columns point to other tables. Fixing a drawing is easier than fixing a database.

What does this query return? Each row shows category and total, rows separated by semicolons.

sales:
item  | category | qty
------+----------+----
Rice  | Food     | 5
Pen   | School   | 10
Beans | Food     | 3
Book  | School   | 4
Soap  | Home     | 2

SELECT category, SUM(qty) FROM sales GROUP BY category ORDER BY category;

Which categories does this query return?

sales:
item  | category | qty
------+----------+----
Rice  | Food     | 5
Pen   | School   | 10
Beans | Food     | 3
Book  | School   | 4
Soap  | Home     | 2

SELECT category FROM sales GROUP BY category HAVING SUM(qty) > 5 ORDER BY category;

What does this query return? The two values are in one row.

sales:
item  | category | qty
------+----------+----
Rice  | Food     | 5
Pen   | School   | 10
Beans | Food     | 3
Book  | School   | 4

SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT category) FROM sales;

The table phones has these rows:

id | model | price
---+-------+------
1  | A     | 100
2  | B     | 200
3  | C     | 300

After this runs, what are the prices of phones 1, 2 and 3 in that order?

UPDATE phones SET price = price + 50 WHERE id > 1;

A shop owner wants to remove only the phone with id 2 from this table:

id | model | price
---+-------+------
1  | A     | 100
2  | B     | 200
3  | C     | 300

The owner types:

DELETE FROM phones;

What happens?
options: All three rows are deleted, because there is no WHERE clause
Only phone 2 is deleted, because it is the second row
Nothing is deleted, because SQL needs a WHERE clause
Only phone 3 is deleted, because it is the last row

quiz.q: You are designing a database for a school library. Which design is best?
options: One big table where every loan repeats the member's full name, class and address
A books table and a members table, with a loans table holding book_id and member_id
A single column that stores all book titles in one text value, separated by commas
A loans table only, with member and book details typed freshly each time
